Add high stakes, lowlifes and a wicked wit, and you've got a solid win.
The play draws its appeal primarily from Bean's tart comic dialogue and the garish charms of the characters as embodied by the superb cast.
It knows its business, hits its marks (or, as the players say, “pots its shots”), and, all in all, makes for a daffy good time.
The comedy can border on mean ("Women can be violent. Joan of Arc. Medea. Naomi Campbell.") but mostly it's laugh-out-loud wacky.
Until the balls fly; then you want to cheer snooker’s first Broadway moment.
Effortful delivery is just one issue with the wheezy direction of Daniel Sullivan, whose forte is definitely not this kind of snappy, suspenseful comedy, in which timing is everything.
The Nap begins to disappoint fast.
Daniel Sullivan’s Broadway production, however, strains mightily to put the show across and succeeds only in whacking it off the table.

Why on earth did anyone think it a good idea to mount a Broadway production of a British farce about a transgender gangster named Waxy Bush who attempts to fix the snooker world tournament—especially one in which all of the characters speak in a mostly unintelligible working-class dialect?
I think I like The Nap even better – it’s sophisticated, adult humor that doesn’t rely on pratfalls or banana peel physicality to get laughs.
Playwright Bean weaves together a bizarre cast of characters and outlandish story strands, creating a tremendously satisfying whole.
David Rockwell’s extravagant set designs are never less than dazzling.

The production (staged with an ear for comic timing and an eye for physical bits by Daniel Sullivan, who is best known for directing contemporary American dramas) is great fun with thick English accents and foul language.
Such is the contagious effect of Bean's odd-ball comedy, a work so refreshingly novel, it defies description.
Clearly, Bean is off and running, and doesn’t disappoint.

You don't need to know much of anything about billiards to get hooked into this witty play from prolific playwright Richard Bean (One Man, Two Guvnors), which came to Broadway after a well-received 2016 run in the U.K.
It's a comedy well timed for the zeitgeist.
He doesn't simply offer a barrage of jokes; he plants them, marinates them, and finally allows them to burst forth at his hapless auditors.
No masterpiece, The Nap, just a traditional, comfortable, fun, funny evening.
If you’re in the mood for a loopy look at game-scamming, a lesson on snooker, and a laugh, The Nap provides an entertaining evening of British-style humor and social farce.
'The Nap' isn't likely to have you napping even though it probably won't make it to the top of your list of really great, long remembered comedies.
After a certain number of jokes, we get it.

The larger problem with “The Nap,” though, is not only that the story turns suddenly darker, but that it ultimately becomes much, much duller -- so much so that there’s even a slight chance your eyes may shut or your mind may wander.
The Nap delivers quirky performances and laugh-out-loud one-liners, but I’ll unlikely be breaking out a cue stick to have my hand at snooker anytime soon.
Sullivan has assembled a first-class cast to portray these seedy second-raters, and everyone gives it his or her all -- which, sometimes, is enough.
For every joke that lands, two don’t – because they’re too silly, or unfathomable, or hackneyed or offensive…in short, in some way unfunny.
It remains consistently, stubbornly, mildly amusing.

The characters are so broadly drawn or hapless that you can’t root for them, you can’t dislike them, you don’t really know them; the plot merely drags them through multiple complications from point A to a kind of incomplete point R.
Pure comedy is back on Broadway.
A superbly comical, poised, and perfectly cast ensemble of kooky characters make this off-beat crime thriller comedy the kind of delightfully droll escape that only theatre can provide.
You will walk away with a favorite, and a few one-liners you pray you will get to use in a conversation.
The fun comes in the collection of the oddball characters and the very amusing writing by Bean, who gives them often-hilarious dialogue to spout and zany situations in which they are placed.
This play is every bit as LOL-excellent as One Man Two Guvnors.
Maybe there is a good reason Richard Bean‘s play, The Nap, has found its way across the pond and into the Friedman Theatre.
Unfortunately, The Nap is not as solid, not as thrilling and is nowhere as hilarious.
Fans of off-beat humor and groan-worthy gags will find some of those pleasures here, but overall the play is overcome by sluggish pacing and hit-or-miss laughs.
It breaks through too rarely, though, to make The Nap as satisfyingly funny as it keeps promising to be.
The biggest question hanging over the Manhattan Theatre Club production is, what are we doing here?
The characters are little more than one-note tics and their interactions just aren’t that funny.
This story of the World Snooker Championship in Sheffield is just dull, a non-entity, a play that was written on autopilot.
It may be early, but I am confident when I say that “The Nap” is the low point of the Broadway season.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this British snooker comedy, with some finding it a hilarious, expertly crafted farce while others call it unfunny and slow-paced. Praise centers on the witty dialogue and strong cast, though many fault the American actors' shaky accents.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
